paragraphs.text: March 13. The martyrdom of Saint Sabinus. When Diocletian was emperor,

a decree was sent throughout the whole world, ordering that all who did not obey his command and did not sacrifice to the gods should be tortured and die a cruel death. This decree reached the whole land of Egypt. While persecution was weighing very heavily upon the Christians and the land of Egypt was in great turmoil, there was at that time a certain man named Sabinus, the leading man of the city of [?], a man of noble birth and renowned name, who was a Christian. Because of the impending danger, he went outside the city and hid in a small hut with other Christians, devoting himself day and night to fasting and prayer. When many Christians had been arrested, and all of them spoke the name of Sabinus with praise, the lawless men made a determined search for him, because they had spoken so highly of the man. A few days later, a certain beggar, who regularly begged for bread and knew the place where Saint Sabinus was living, came and said to the lawless men, “What will you give me if I show you the place where Sabinus, whom you are seeking, is staying?” When they heard this, they were glad and gave him two gold coins. They followed him and reached the place. They knocked at the door as though behaving foolishly. One of the brothers opened it, wanting to find out what they wanted. Immediately the lawless men rushed in and found Saint Sabinus with six other

brothers. They bound them and dragged them out of the room. They asked which of them was Sabinus, whom they were seeking. When they found out, they took him alone and bound him with two sets of chains. They put heavy wooden stocks on him and brought him to the governor. At that time a certain man named Arian was governor in the city called [?]. He went out for a ride along the river and saw in the distance a great crowd of people approaching. Seeing a pleasant, grassy place, he dismounted from his horse to relax. After a short time, he raised his eyes and saw Saint Sabinus being dragged along with great violence. He said to the clerk, “Who is the man whom the soldiers of our command are bringing?” The clerk replied, “I think, my lord governor, that he is one of the poor Christians.” A little later the soldiers arrived and stood before the governor. They approached the clerk, saying, “Is this Sabinus, the protector of the Christians, whom your—your authority has been seeking from the beginning?” When he heard this, he was overjoyed and said: Thanks to the merciful and immortal gods. And immediately he ordered a throne to be set up in a high place. And sitting on the high seat, he said, “Sabinus, who belongs to the impious faith, who is called a Christian, an insolent man—

let him be brought before our tribunal.” The court secretary said, “Your Majesty ordered Sabinus to be kept in prison. But if you command it, he will appear before your tribunal.” When he had been brought in, Arianus the governor said, “First let him declare his name and his station, and where he comes from.” Saint Sabinus said, “My name is Sabinus, and I am a Christian.” The governor said, “Are you a slave or a free man?” Sabinus said, “I am free, in the prime of life, and a soldier in the spiritual ranks.” The governor said, “What happened to you that you left your military service, rather than put yourself in order and make yourself useful to the sacred emperors and their laws?” Saint Sabinus answered, “When I saw their lawless commands reaching the servants of Christ, I chose rather to remain at the threshold of the house of my God than to live in the dwellings of sinners.” The governor said, “Have you not heard what the emperors have commanded us: that everyone, everywhere, in every province, region, and place, must sacrifice and make offerings to the merciful gods?” Sabinus said, “The impious command has not escaped our notice, as I said before, nor have the laws, because of which they led many astray and destroyed them. And you call the emperors [?], since by a thing [?]

those laws of yours are true [?]. For they do this without understanding, blaspheming their own Lord and benefactor. But I sacrifice to my God Jesus Christ, and I serve him alone.” Arianus the governor became angry and said, “You wicked man, have you dared to insult our good emperors and their sacred laws, which they have issued to us for the salvation of all?” Sabinus said, “Know well, governor, that I will never sacrifice to your gods, even if you command it with every threat.” Hearing this, the governor said, “Even now, however, I am treating you mercifully, because of the mercy of the immortal gods. Acknowledge, then, that they are true and beneficent gods. Otherwise, the punishments and tortures that you will suffer at my hands will make you know that they are true gods.” Saint Sabinus answered, “You will by no means [?] me by threatening me with torture.” The governor said, “The sacred and revered laws command that you be subjected to various tortures if you persist in disobedience.” Saint Sabinus said, “If we are so afraid of earthly torments and punishment, which, though they are many, cannot forever and always hold the person tortured in this way over sacrificing

to worthless gods, how much more ought we to fear Christ Jesus, who can, through the torments he has prepared for the lawless, hold forever all those who have not opposed him. We ought therefore to fear God more, and our Lord Jesus Christ, rather than these so-called gods, who are worthless.” When Arianus the governor heard this, he said, “See, I have taught you how to understand and confess that there are gods. Otherwise, I will compel you to confess against your will. Confess willingly, then, before suffering comes.” Saint Sabinus said, “You compel me to say that those you speak of are gods. Likewise, I will compel you, before all these people, to confess that there is a God in heaven, and that there is no other besides him, except Christ Jesus, the God of Sabinus.” Hearing this, the governor became very angry and ordered them to hang him up and scrape his flesh. The holy martyr of God was scraped so severely that all his flesh fell to the ground. Then the governor said, “Have you still not submitted to sacrificing to the gods?” Saint Sabinus answered, “I will certainly not sacrifice.” Then one of those standing nearby, named Visambon, said, “Our lord, he cannot stand, but is about to breathe his last and die.” When Sabinus heard this, he immediately cried out, saying, “I have not lost my mind, nor has my understanding failed,

so that I should turn away from God who created me—may that never happen!” Arianus the governor said, “Are you still defiant and hard-hearted, Sabinus? But I will not torture you here. Let us go to the other side, to Antinoopolis, so that there you may learn that the gods to whom the emperors command us to sacrifice are true gods.” Sabinus was taken to Antinoopolis ahead of the governor. After crossing the river, he became weak and remained there under guard on the riverbank. Great crowds came out of the city to see the blessed martyr. Meanwhile, the governor boarded a boat, intending to cross over to Antinoopolis, where Saint Sabinus had been taken. When the holy martyr of God heard the crowds standing around him saying that the governor had boarded the boat, As he was about to come into this city, he rose, and standing in the midst of all the people, he prayed, saying, “My God, Christ Jesus, for whose sake I have endured this suffering and become a spectacle, and am seen naked by so many people, hear me today and stretch out your mighty hand, and glorify your name and me, your sinful, unworthy servant, in the midst of these people. Thus may your holy name be glorified. Bring the lawless governor to a halt in the middle of the river, and keep his boat from crossing, but let him be in distress, so that perhaps, compelled by necessity, he may glorify your honored and great name,

which he denies.” As soon as Sabinus said this, the boat stopped in the middle of the river and was tossed about violently. When the governor realized this, he said to those who were with him in the boat, “You see that what that sorcerer said, he has accomplished through sorcery, and he is holding us in the middle of the river. I am astonished to see the power of his sorcery.” Then the governor ordered other boats to be summoned to his aid. Those in the boat shouted and called for boats to come to their aid. But when they reached the place where the governor’s boat was, they too were violently battered by the winds and waves and turned back. They were in distress. One of their boats, unable to approach the governor’s boat, turned toward the other bank. Then the governor called out to those in the boat, saying, “Go to the other bank and look outside the city for a certain man named Sabinus, a Christian who has been tortured, and say to him, ‘Why have you used your sorcery to stop us from coming across to you?’ For he was afraid of torture, and that is why he would not let us cross.” Those in the boat went, and finding Saint Sabinus, they said to him those words. The saint answered them, “As the Lord my God Jesus Christ lives, for whose sake I am suffering these things, he shall not cross to the other bank until

he first confesses the name of my Lord Jesus Christ.” Then a certain soldier named Hermias, one of those guarding him, said to him, “How can you know, being so far away, whether the governor confesses?” Saint Sabinus answered, saying, “When he writes a letter confessing my God and sends it to me before all of you, then he too will be allowed to enter the city.” When they returned and came with the boat close to the governor, And they told him everything they had heard from Saint Sabinus, for they had already despaired of their lives. And he asked for a sheet of papyrus and wrote this: “There is one God, the God of Sabinus, Jesus Christ, and there is no other besides him.” And when he had written this and sent it to Saint Sabinus, immediately it grew calm, and the ship sped toward the other shore. The governor entered the city, sat on the judgment seat, and ordered Saint Sabinus to be brought before him. And he said to him, “You have begun a deed hated by the gods and the emperors, you who held us in the middle of the river by your sorcery. For you did to me as much as you could, just as you wished. So I will do to you what I can.” And he ordered lighted torches to be brought and the martyr to be stretched out with four ropes and tied to four stakes,

and his belly and sides to be burned, until his flesh, burned like wax, melted away. Although so much suffering was inflicted on him, he did not utter a single cry, but continued to endure, as though someone else were suffering and not he himself. Arianus the governor said: “You fool, tell me, what [?] is to happen, since you feel nothing at all, though you are being tortured so very cruelly? What do you hope for, or in whom do you trust? Tell me.” Saint Sabinus answered, “I place my hope in my God, Jesus Christ, for he is able to deliver me from your futile tortures and make me worthy of the eternal kingdom.” The governor said, “Do you wish, then, to die a terrible death?” The martyr of Christ answered, saying, “Even if I die, I still have eternal life, as I said.” When Arianus the governor heard this, he became angry and said to the soldiers, “See, the sun and moon are your witnesses to how and why I tortured this wicked man. And let all of you who live in this city know that he would not repent at all or sacrifice to the gods so that he might be saved, but chose instead to die under torture. So now let sentence be passed upon him.” And having said this, he ordered him to be thrown into the river and to die in its depths.

The soldiers took him and led him to the riverbank. And they took a large stone and tied it to his feet, to throw him into the river in this way, according to the governor’s sentence. Some of the many brothers brought him food to eat. But he said, “Why do you trouble yourselves, beloved? From now on I will no longer taste earthly food.” But I await the taste of that food which no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered the human heart. And I want all of you to follow after me. And seeing me struggle in this way, may you too be worthy to receive the crown of eternal life. When he had said this, the soldiers brought him into the boat, along with the stone which they had tied to his feet. And when he was in the middle of the river, he cried out again to those standing there and to the crowd watching him, saying: “Look at me and remember me. And after [?], come in the morning on the third day, and on the north side of the city you will find my body cast onto dry land. And this stone which I have on my foot, I want you to bury with my body.” Having said this, the holy martyr of God, Sabinus, looked up to heaven and prayed, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, glory to you for what you have done for me, your unworthy servant.
